steps.action:
# DNA vs. RNA: Key Differences

## Structure

**DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid)**
- Double-stranded helix (two complementary strands wound together)
- Contains the sugar **deoxyribose** (missing one oxygen atom)
- Uses the bases: Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, Cytosine (A, T, G, C)

**RNA (Ribonucleic Acid)**
- Generally **single-stranded**
- Contains the sugar **ribose** (has an extra hydroxyl -OH group)
- Uses the bases: Adenine, **Uracil**, Guanine, Cytosine (A, **U**, G, C) — Uracil replaces Thymine

---

## Function

**DNA** serves as the **long-term storage** of genetic information — essentially the master blueprint of an organism. It stays mostly in the nucleus and is replicated when cells divide.

**RNA** acts as a **working copy and messenger**, carrying instructions from DNA out to the rest of the cell. It also plays structural and catalytic roles.

---

## Types of RNA
- **mRNA** — carries genetic code to ribosomes
- **tRNA** — delivers amino acids during protein building
- **rRNA** — structural component of ribosomes
- **Others** — regulatory roles (siRNA, miRNA, etc.)

---

## Stability
- DNA is **more stable** — suited for long-term information storage
- RNA is **less stable** — intentionally short-lived for flexible regulation

---

## Simple Summary
> **DNA is the archive; RNA is the working document.**
